extracted.intended_audience: poets, students and scholars of poetics and classical literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for composing/assessing epic and tragic poetry (diction, meter, plot unity, use of names/metaphor, sound/euphony, and genre-appropriate devices) based on classical poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of utterance (elementa eloquii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllaba, coniunctio, separativa, nomen, verbum, casus, sermo (the basic elements of speech/poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand each element's role for composition and metrical effect: syllables and their parts (vowel, non-vowel, semi-vowel) determine metrical possibility; conjunctions and particles form non-significant compound sounds used at beginnings/middles; nouns, verbs, cases and sentences carry semantic/temporal meaning relevant to poetic construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic/metrical suitability of sounds (syllable types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish vocal, non-vocal, and semi-vocal sounds and how their combinations create syllables and affect metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for how sounds vary with mouth shape, place, aspiration, length, quantity and weight; certain sound-combinations form audible syllables (e.g., GRA) only with vowels and so influence meter. Inspect variations for metric practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of parts of speech (nomen/verbum/casus/sententia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nouns, verbs, cases and sentences have definable semantic/time properties: verbs indicate tense, nouns may be simple/compound, and sentences can be meaningful without verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use word classes deliberately: verbs to signal time (present, past, future), cases to indicate role in sentence, and compose sentences whose parts may each signify separately; definitions and examples (e.g., 'homo', 'ambulat') illustrate permissible constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of diction (λέξεως ἀρετή σαφῆ καὶ μὴ ταπεινὴν)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction's virtue is to be clear (saphes) and not low/vulgar (mē tapeinēn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity and avoid base or excessively colloquial expressions. Diction should be chaste and intelligible to the intended audience; examples contrast celebrated (famous) diction with low usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity and controlled variety (σεμνὴ καὶ ἐξαλλάττουσα τὸ ἰδιωτικὸν)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use foreign words, metaphors, extensions and ornament (gloss, translatio, ornamentum) to achieve majesty and variation from the ordinary, but in measured amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate use of glosses, translations and metaphors enriches diction; overuse (all such devices at once) produces either an enigma (if metaphorical) or barbarism (if from tongues/dialects). The devices should not render meaning obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of transferred names and metaphors (translatio/glossa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferred names (from genus to species, species to genus, analogical transfers) and metaphors must be apt and analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good transference requires skill — it signals craft when applied to like things; poor or ignorant transfer causes ridicule. Use such transfers to create apt imagery (examples in text: metaphorical uses like 'myriad' for many).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-lexical matching (names/glosses/metaphors ↔ meter/genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain lexical types suit particular metres/genres: duplicated names suit dithyramb, glosses suit heroic/recitative metres, and transferred names suit iambic (imitative) metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match lexical choices to the meter and genre: e.g., double-form names for dithyrambs, glossa for heroic recitations, transferred terms for iambic composition. Misalignment will feel inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ridicule through inappropriate language choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Using dialects, metaphors or foreign terms in a way that is at odds with established usage or audience expectation provokes derision (ridiculum) and may make the poet seem ignorant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt strange dialectal forms or misplace names where they are not customary for the audience; improper or forced use of such items produces comic effect rather than dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euphony and balance of name endings/phonetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance masculine/feminine and intermediate name endings and respect phonetic conventions (which letters mark genders and how many names end in resting letters) to maintain euphony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider phonetic endings (e.g., masculine endings by certain consonants, feminine by long vowels) so masculine and feminine names balance in number and sound; such euphony contributes to a polished diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (one whole action with beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic (tragedy) or mimetic narrative should be a whole: a complete single action having a beginning, middle and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose plots so the audience can perceive the start and the finish as parts of one whole; avoid episodic aggregations that lack a unified telos. Examples: tragedies should represent one complete action in one course of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal unity (single course of time for the action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action should concern a single time-span (one unified period) rather than multiple unrelated times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narratives that stitch together events from different times without a unifying principle; episodic assemblages (many events across disparate times) fail to produce a single coherent dramatic end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale and length for genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic (epopoiia) is naturally larger than tragedy; length must be sufficient to make beginning and ending visible but not so diffuse as to lose unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scope so that the work's beginning and end are perceivable. Epic can accommodate many episodes via narration; tragedy is constrained to what can be shown on stage and by actors. Excessive extension can produce satiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate inclusion of episode/narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic may include many narrated episodes (increasing bulk and variety); tragedy should confine itself to what is enacted and appropriate to the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narration to expand epic scope; rely on enacted parts and actor performance in tragedy. Do not attempt to imitate epic’s multi-part narration in tragedy where stage limitations and unity demand restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential incidents and devices (reversal, recognition, pathos, thought, diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy (and epic in their way) requires occurrences of peripeteia (reversal), anagnorisis (recognition), pathē (suffering/pathos), well-formed thought and suitable diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include well-structured incidents of reversal and recognition to produce pathos; craft thought and diction carefully to support emotional and intellectual effect. These features are central to tragic success and should be well integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter must suit the imitation and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different metres fit different kinds of imitation: heroic metre befits grand/epic material, iambic/tetrameter suits mimetic/kinetic and practical uses; mixing incompatible metres is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select meter by experience and natural fit to the subject matter; avoid lengthy systems in a metre alien to the poem. Example: heroic metre is grand and weighty and thus appropriate to epic; iambic suits imitation of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and immediacy in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should say little and introduce persons/actions promptly — brief prooemia and immediate entry into the action (as Homer does).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise introductions; introduce characters swiftly and avoid superfluous exposition. Economical handling keeps the imitation direct and avoids the imitator’s excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the marvelous and novelty to engage the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of the marvelous (thaumaston) and varied, dissimilar introductions keeps the audience engaged and prevents satiety, especially in epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ marvels/novelty strategically to change and delight the listener; avoid repetitive similarity which quickly produces satiety. Tragedy requires some marvel; epic allows and benefits more expansive marvellous elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing incompatible stylistic devices gratuitously
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not combine incongruous dialects, meters, or rhetorical devices just to show skill — such mixing can be disorderly and improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let nature of the material and genre guide choices; arbitrary mingling (e.g., of heroic metre with iambic imitation) looks odd and detracts from unity and suitability.
